questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Defining Culture: Wholes and Parts' refers to.
questions.a: Culture is the whole way of life of a people -- learned and shared beliefs, values, norms, language and material objects. Its parts interlock: material culture (tools, dress, buildings) and non-material culture (ideas, customs) change together, so studying one part always implicates the rest.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Defining Culture: Wholes and Parts'.
questions.a: Culture is the learned and shared design for living -- objects and ideas woven into one whole.

concepts.title: Dimensions of Culture: Cognitive, Normative and Beliefs

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Dimensions of Culture: Cognitive, Normative and Beliefs' refers to.
questions.a: Culture works through three dimensions. Cognitive culture is what people know and how they think -- categories, language, knowledge. Normative culture is what they ought to do -- values and norms. Symbolic culture is the meanings attached to things -- a flag, a colour, a gesture -- through which beliefs about the world and the sacred are expressed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Dimensions of Culture: Cognitive, Normative and Beliefs'.
questions.a: Culture tells you what is (cognition), what ought to be (norms) and what things mean (symbols).

questions.q: Under which section is 'Dimensions of Culture: Cognitive, Normative and Beliefs' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Socialisation: Becoming a Member of Society

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Socialisation: Becoming a Member of Society' refers to.
questions.a: Socialisation is the lifelong process by which the newborn biological being becomes a social person -- learning language, norms, roles and selfhood through interaction. Primary socialisation in the family forms the basic personality; later phases through school, peers and media continuously resocialise the individual into new roles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Socialisation: Becoming a Member of Society'.
questions.a: Nobody is born social -- interaction turns the infant into a person, and the process never stops.

concepts.title: Identity, Self and the Individual in Society

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Identity, Self and the Individual in Society' refers to.
questions.a: The self is socially formed: we come to know who we are through others' expectations and responses, acquiring identities -- gender, caste, nationality, profession -- that position us in society. Individuality and society are not enemies; the distinctive person matures only inside a web of social relationships.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Identity, Self and the Individual in Society'.
questions.a: The mirror of society builds the self -- identities are socially given, yet each person assembles them uniquely.
